changes.before: Two revisions have the same total pass count. Can you conclude they behave identically?
changes.after: After a change, compare individual test results as well as the total score.

before: A regression set is a collection of representative cases used again after a change. It helps detect when an improvement in one area breaks behavior elsewhere.
Suppose a prompt change improves short summaries but starts omitting dates. Keep ordinary summaries, date-sensitive summaries, and previously failing cases in the evaluation set.

Worked example: revision A passes 18 of 20 fixed cases. Revision B also passes 18, but fails two different important cases. Equal totals do not mean equal behavior; compare the individual results and their consequences.

Record the input, expected criteria, model or prompt version, and actual outcome. Keep separate held-out cases so repeated tuning on the regression set does not become the only measure of generalization. No finite set proves universal correctness.
Changed situation: Two revisions have the same total pass count. Can you conclude they behave identically?
The same count can conceal different failures. Case-level evidence and failure importance matter.
after: A regression is something that worked before but stops working after a change. A regression set is a collection of cases you test again to look for this problem.
Choose cases that reflect real tasks and earlier failures. Write down what counts as passing before comparing versions.
The totals match, but the date check changed from passing to failing. The name check improved. Compare which results changed and why each matters.
Record the input, pass criteria, model and prompt versions, and actual results. Repeat checks when results can vary, so one lucky answer does not hide a problem.
Keep fresh held-out cases too. Repeatedly changing a model to fit the same regression set can hide poor performance on new cases. No finite set of tests proves every future answer will be correct.
